# Data and preprocessing methods

*This section is written to be reused in the project report. Every number is regenerated by
`bash scripts/run_all.sh`, and the per-step evidence is in the files under `reports/`.*

## Groundwater data

The groundwater data come from the openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) dataset "Quality controlled, reliable
groundwater level data with corresponding specific yield over India" (Figshare,
doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.29293877.v3). Its source is manual water-level measurements by the Central
Ground Water Board (CGWB). CGWB measures each monitoring well four times a year, in January, May,
August and November. We treat these rounds as four seasons: post-monsoon (rabi), pre-monsoon,
monsoon and post-monsoon (kharif). Each value is the depth to groundwater in metres below ground
level, so a larger value means a deeper water table and more stress. The download contains the raw
CGWB table for 2000–2024 and the dataset authors' successive quality-control outputs.

We use the authors' refined table, `CGWB_India_filtered_GWLs_ref_sy_2000_2022.csv`. It covers
2,759 wells in 19 states and 365 districts, matching the counts in the authors' paper, and each well
has 92 rounds from January 2000 to November 2022. Of the 253,828 well-round cells, 219,258 hold a
reading and 13.62% are empty. Missingness is very uneven over time. The May rounds of 2020 and
2021, during the COVID-19 period, have readings for only 0.9% of wells. August 2012 has 2.5%, and
January 2016 has 19.1%. In addition, 444 wells have no May reading in any year: every well in
Kerala and West Bengal, 189 of 191 in Odisha, and all 16 in Assam. No well has all four rounds
filled in every year; the median well has 15 complete years out of 23.

The table's own station identifier, `Station Code`, was damaged upstream when it was saved in
scientific notation. In the refined table only 2,411 of 2,759 codes are distinct, and only 182 are
distinct in the copy that carries specific yield. We therefore built a surrogate key, `well_id`. It
is a SHA-1 hash of the state, district, station name and coordinates, which are unique for every
well. A crosswalk keeps both corrupted versions of the original code for anyone who needs to match
back to CGWB records.

The refined table also gives each well a specific yield (`Reference_Sy`). The authors assigned it
by clustering the colours of a hydrogeological map at the well location into five aquifer classes.
We keep it as a categorical aquifer-class covariate, not as a measured quantity.

## Quality control by the dataset authors

According to their ReadMe and processing notebook, the dataset authors applied five criteria in
order.

1. They removed wells with no readings at all. Despite its file name, this step did not remove
   readings equal to zero.
2. They removed every well that had any negative reading.
3. For each well, they blanked readings more than three standard deviations from that well's mean.
   The mean and standard deviation came from the whole 2000–2024 series, so this step uses the
   complete record; it is quality control, not a model feature.
4. They kept only wells with at least two of the four rounds filled in every year of the target
   period.
5. They removed wells in which any value repeated more than twice in a row, which suggests a stuck
   gauge or values copied forward.

Specific yield was then attached to the wells that remained. Applying criteria 4 and 5 over
2000–2022 is what produces the 2,759 wells. The same procedure over 2000–2024 leaves only 399 wells
in 5 states, which is why we chose the 2000–2022 table.

## Our cleaning

We did not remove outliers a second time. The authors' 3σ step had already done so, and a second
pass would discard genuine extremes, which are exactly what a stress study needs to keep. The
cleaning rules we did apply removed nothing from this table:

- **Placeholders and duplicates.** Placeholder values (−999 and similar, or non-finite values) are
  converted to missing, and exact duplicate rows are dropped. Neither occurred.
- **Names.** State and district names were standardised: 6 state names and 31 district names
  changed, all in capitalisation only.
- **Wells.** We kept all 2,759 wells. Every well has at least 57 of 92 readings, so a cut-off on the
  total number of readings would only have thrown away data.

The value convention was checked directly. All readings are non-negative depths below ground,
ranging from 0 to 66.9 m with a median of 4.6 m, and none follows a different sign convention.
Several conditions are flagged but left unchanged:

- **Zero readings.** There are 11 readings of exactly 0.0 m. Eight of them fall in the August
  (monsoon) rounds of 2019 and 2020 and are consistent with a full well. Three are isolated zeros
  between much deeper readings (Ujjain, August 2019; Raisen, November 2019; Nellore, January 2018)
  and are marked as suspicious.
- **Deeper than the well.** 537 readings in 246 wells are deeper than the well's recorded depth. On
  inspection these mostly reflect an outdated depth record rather than bad readings. The clearest
  case is a Kanpur Dehat well that falls smoothly from 8 m to 19 m against a recorded depth of
  14 m.
- **Composite flag.** `suspect_reading` combines the three suspicious zeros, the readings deeper
  than the well, and readings with an absolute anomaly above 5. It flags 2,135 readings (0.97%).
  It is meant for sensitivity analysis, not deletion.

Coordinate checks found no wells outside India's extent and no exactly co-located wells. One pair,
in Chanderi, Madhya Pradesh, is about 100 m apart.

## Rainfall data

Monthly rainfall comes from CHIRPS v3.0 (Climate Hazards Center), a global 0.05° grid. We
downloaded it over HTTPS one file at a time, sampled it at every well, and deleted each raster
immediately; no raster was kept or committed. Each well takes the value of the grid cell that
contains it, and nodata or negative values are treated as missing. The record runs from July 1999
to December 2022: 282 months and 778,038 well-month values, none of them missing.

To check whether one cell represents its surroundings, we repeated the extraction and also
recorded the mean of the surrounding 3×3 block of cells, about 16 × 16 km. The two agree closely,
with a correlation of 0.9991 and a mean absolute difference of 3.43 mm per month, or 2.7% of mean
monthly rainfall. No well's 3×3 block touches the coast or the edge of the raster. The 13 wells
with large differences all lie on steep rainfall gradients: the Palghat gap, Wayanad, the Darjeeling
foothills, Kangra and Kullu, the Karjat ghat, and the Yercaud and Kodaikanal hills. At such sites
the 3×3 mean pulls in rain from a neighbouring ridge. We therefore kept the nearest cell as the
primary source and keep the 3×3 table for sensitivity analyses.

A plausibility check found no implausible state totals. The lowest Jun–Sep totals belong to eight
wells in the rain shadow of western Tamil Nadu. The highest annual totals, above 7,000 mm, come from
the Western Ghats crest in Udupi.

## Leakage controls

CGWB reports the month of each reading but not the day. Rainfall later in the same month may
therefore have fallen after the measurement, so for a reading in month M every rainfall feature
ends at month M−1. All rainfall windows are built through two functions that assert, on every row
and on every run, that no month at or after the observation month contributes. A unit test feeds
these functions a deliberately leaky configuration and confirms that they raise an error.

Every groundwater feature uses only readings from earlier rounds of the same well. Static
attributes are allowed. The one exception is the anomaly, a transformation of the current reading,
which is treated as a label rather than an input. A perturbation test replaces all readings and
all monthly rainfall from a cutoff date onward with wildly different values. It then checks that
every feature of every earlier row is unchanged, at four cutoffs (January, May, August and
November 2006) and for every column in the table. A companion test shows that this check fails on
a deliberately leaky column. The only columns exempt are three documented descriptive columns
that use the whole record by design: a robust outlier flag, full-period completeness, and a flag
for wells with no series in a season. They are marked as never-to-be-used inputs.

## Features

All features are past-only.

- **Rainfall windows.** Totals over the 1, 3 and 6 complete months before the reading, plus a
  12-month total.
- **Monsoon rainfall.** The total of the most recent completed Jun–Sep monsoon, and the total of the
  most recent completed Oct–Dec north-east monsoon, which is always the previous year's. Rainfall
  since 1 June of the current monsoon year is also included.
- **Rainfall deviations.** Each rainfall feature's deviation from the well's own normal, computed
  only over earlier years with at least five of them, as millimetres, percentages and capped
  z-scores.
- **Groundwater history.** The previous round's reading, the same season one and two years earlier,
  the latest observed change, the deepest and shallowest readings so far, the number of readings so
  far, and the previous water year's May-to-November change.
- **Trend.** A Theil-Sen slope over the same season's readings in the five previous years, needing
  at least four of them.
- **Completeness and calendar.** The share of earlier rounds observed, the water year, and the
  position of the round within it.

The Oct–Dec features were added because monsoon timing differs sharply between states. Tamil Nadu
receives 41.4% of its rain in Oct–Dec and 40.1% in Jun–Sep, Andhra Pradesh receives 27.1% in Oct–Dec,
and every state outside the south receives under 12% then.

## Seasonal baseline, anomaly and stress classification

Groundwater levels follow a strong seasonal cycle, so each reading is compared only with earlier
readings of the same well in the same season. The primary baseline is expanding: the mean and
standard deviation (ddof = 1) of all earlier same-season readings. The anomaly is the reading minus
the baseline mean, divided by the standard deviation. The standard deviation is floored at 0.10 m,
roughly the precision of manual tape readings, so that nearly constant records cannot produce
extreme scores; the floor applied to 251 rows. Raw anomalies have heavy tails, from −56 to +39, so
a version capped at ±5 is provided for modelling.

**Minimum-history rule.** No baseline is computed until a well has at least K earlier readings in
the same season, and a z-score is never computed from one or two readings. With the chosen K = 5,
52,952 readings (24.2%) have no baseline. With K = 3 the figure is 14.5%, and with K = 8 it is
38.6%. Almost all excluded readings are each well-season's first few, so labels effectively begin
around 2005.

**Stress classes.** A reading's stress class comes from its anomaly. Because a positive anomaly
means a deeper-than-usual water table, the classes are:

| Anomaly z | Class |
|---|---|
| below 1 | Normal |
| 1 to below 1.5 | Watch |
| 1.5 to below 2 | Moderate Stress |
| 2 or more | High Stress |

A shallower-than-usual reading is Normal, not a separate class. Rounds without a reading are
labelled "No reading", and readings without a baseline are labelled "Insufficient history". The
thresholds are parameters. Moving to 0.5/1/1.5 changes 23.5% of classified labels, 1.5/2/2.5
changes 14.7%, and 1/2/3 changes 8.5%. Under the default thresholds, classified readings are 81.5%
Normal, 7.6% Watch, 4.5% Moderate Stress and 6.4% High Stress.

## Methodological findings on the High Stress rate

Under a standard normal distribution, 2.28% of readings would exceed z = 2, but the expanding
baseline puts 6.38% of classified readings in High Stress. We tested two explanations.

**Baseline lag.** The first explanation was that the expanding mean lags behind wells in long-term
decline, so their recent readings look anomalous. We replaced it with a rolling baseline (the last
10 earlier same-season readings, minimum 5, same floor and thresholds). This did not lower the
High Stress rate; it raised it slightly to 6.90%, and labels differed on 6.6% of readings. Baseline
lag is not the main cause. Indeed, a steady linear decline does not inflate the expanding z-score:
the lag of the mean grows, but the spread of earlier readings grows at the same rate, so the score
levels off near a constant of about 1.7.

**Small samples.** The second explanation is the size of the sample. With only n earlier readings,
the baseline mean and standard deviation are themselves uncertain. Even for independent Gaussian
data, a standardised new reading follows a Student-t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom,
scaled by √(1 + 1/n). Its tails are much heavier than normal at n = 5 to 10, so z ≥ 2 occurs 4.7–6.3%
of the time instead of 2.28%.

We added an adjusted score, anomaly_tadj. It computes t = (x − mean) / (s·√(1 + 1/n)) and converts
it to a normal-equivalent value through the t and normal distribution functions. A Monte Carlo test
on independent Gaussian data confirms that the adjusted score has nominal tail rates at n = 5 and
n = 8, while the unadjusted score exceeds them by more than 1.8 times. On the real data the
adjustment lowers High Stress from 6.38% to 4.18%, removing 54% of the excess over the nominal
rate. The 10,611 readings (6.4%) whose class changes all move towards Normal.

The remaining excess is concentrated in particular years, mainly 2015–2018 and 2009, which is
consistent with drought-driven declines after the deficient 2009 and 2014–2015 monsoons. It also
reflects serial correlation, trends and heavy tails, which the adjustment does not model. We do not
attribute it to any single cause. The expanding-baseline label stays the primary label; the
adjusted and rolling labels are provided as sensitivity variants.

## Extension holdout, 2023–2024

The refined wells were chosen for their completeness through 2022, so the most recent rounds of
the main table are slightly pre-selected for quality. As an additional, independent holdout we
extracted the January 2023 to November 2024 rounds for the same 2,759 wells from the authors'
earlier stage-4 table, which has passed only the first three QC criteria.

All 2,759 wells were matched with the same surrogate key, with no unmatched wells and no coordinate
mismatches. For every matched well, the 2000–2022 readings in the stage-4 table equal the main table
exactly, which proves the match. One well appeared twice in the stage-4 table; the duplicate was a
sparse twin, resolved by that exact-equality test.

The extension readings did not pass the repeated-value filter or the at-least-two-readings-per-year
rule. Their coverage is also much lower: 30.9% of cells against 80.0% in 2018–2022, falling from
69.8% in January 2023 to 8.0% in November 2024, with no readings at all for Delhi. They also contain
87 zero readings (68 of them in May 2023) against 11 in all of 2000–2022. These look like placeholder
values and are flagged.

Extension features were computed with the same code on the combined 2000–2024 series, using CHIRPS
rainfall extended to December 2024 (nearest cell only). We also recomputed the main table from this
combined data and confirmed that every 2000–2022 row is unchanged in every past-only column. This is
a second, end-to-end demonstration that the features use no future information. The extension is
stored separately and never mixed into the main table.

## Evaluation splits

A single splits file marks each row as eligible for evaluation when three conditions hold: a reading
exists, a baseline exists under K = 5, and the round is not sparse. A round counts as sparse when
fewer than 70% of wells were measured, or fewer than 15% for the extension rounds, whose coverage is
low by construction. Seven main rounds are excluded as sparse (May 2020, May 2021, August 2012,
January 2016, August 2020, May 2016 and November 2018), along with three extension rounds.

The file also gives a chronological assignment and a state fold. The chronological split puts
2000–2015 in train, 2016–2017 in validation, 2018–2022 in test and 2023–2024 in the extension, with
104,437, 15,513, 40,630 and 5,989 eligible rows respectively. The state fold gives each of the 19
states an integer, for leave-states-out evaluation of cross-region generalisation. A per-well flag
marks the 444 wells without a May series. All cutoffs live in one configuration file.

## Known limitations

- **Missing rounds.** Several monitoring rounds are almost empty, so some season-years have no
  labels.
- **No pre-monsoon labels in four states.** Kerala, West Bengal, Odisha and Assam have no
  pre-monsoon labels at all.
- **Late-starting labels.** Labels begin around 2005 because of the minimum-history rule.
- **Residual excess High Stress.** Even after the small-sample adjustment, High Stress remains above
  its nominal rate.
- **Tamil Nadu rainfall timing.** Jun–Sep rainfall carries little signal for Tamil Nadu.
- **Unknown reading day.** The day of each reading is unknown.
- **Corrupted station codes.** The original station codes are corrupted, and well depths may be
  outdated.
- **Lower-quality extension.** The extension holdout has lower coverage, likely placeholder zeros,
  and less upstream filtering.

## Reproducibility

The whole pipeline is a sequence of scripts over committed inputs: the dataset files, the three
CHIRPS tables and a configuration file. A single command, `bash scripts/run_all.sh`, regenerates
every output and report without downloading anything, and ends with the 59-test suite. Package
versions are pinned in `requirements.txt`. A machine-readable data contract fixes the class, type,
range and missing-value policy of every column, and is enforced by contract tests that also check
key uniqueness, the 2,759 × 92 grid, one-to-one joins between all files, and a 50 MB limit per
committed file. The column dictionary in the modelling handoff is generated from the same contract.

We verified reproduction by cloning the repository fresh, deleting all generated outputs, and
running the single command (3 minutes). A comparison script then found zero differences in all 18
outputs and reports against the committed versions, comparing Parquet contents with a 1e-9 float
tolerance and text exactly. The CHIRPS download scripts are separate, resumable, polite (sequential
with back-off), and never keep rasters on disk.
